verdict.rationale: Across the canon the figure named by H7854 satan, G1228 diabolos, and G4567 satanas consistently occupies the grammatical slot of a personal agent. In Job 1 to 2 the satan is the Subject of speech verbs, answers Yahweh with H6030, and is addressed with H0559 plus H0413 across nine verses. In Matt 4, Mark 1 and 3, Luke 4, 10, 11 and 22, the figure approaches, stands, takes, shows, departs, and speaks, with verbs like G2476, G3880, G1166, G2980, G2036 attaching to the named subject. John 8:44 predicates the personal-relational and moral nouns father, murderer, liar of him. 1 Pet 5:8 calls him antidikos and seeking to devour. Rev 12:9 and Rev 20:2 stack dragon, ancient serpent, Diabolos, and Satanas onto one referent who deceives and is bound. The personal-agent and opposer-of-God clauses hold pan-canonically with dense, recurring grammar. The created clause is not directly carried by these anchor lemmas, so it rests on inference from wider canon and is recorded honestly as a residual.

scripture.force: The satan comes among the sons of God to present himself before Yahweh. H0935, the verb of coming, takes the satan as its personal subject, placing him as one acting agent within a council scene of agents rather than as an abstraction.

Yahweh says to the satan using H0559 with the directional H0413, and the satan answers Yahweh using H6030. Two-way address with a named respondent is grammar that requires a personal interlocutor, not a force or principle. The same speech grammar continues in Job.1.8, Job.1.9, Job.1.12, Job.2.2, Job.2.3, Job.2.4, and Job.2.6.

Yahweh hands what Job has into the satan's hand, and the satan then goes out from the presence of Yahweh. Possession of agency, recipient of permission, and locomotion are predicated of the referent. These are agent attributes, not properties of a personification.

The satan stands at the right hand of the high priest to accuse him, with H5975 taking the satan as Subject. Standing and accusing are agent verbs. The same accusatory frame recurs in Ps 109:6 where a satan is set against an enemy in a courtroom register.

Satan, here for the first time without the article in Hebrew narrative, stands up against Israel and incites David. The anarthrous form moves the lexeme toward a name rather than a title, and the verb of inciting H5496 takes the satan as personal subject acting upon a human king.

The tempter, ho peirazon, the participial designation of the same figure introduced in verse 1 as ho diabolos, comes near and speaks, with proselthon then eipen. The pairing of approach and speech is the standard Greek frame for a personal speaker.

The diabolos takes Jesus to the holy city and stands him on the pinnacle, with G3880 and G2476 as transitive verbs of physical action. A figurative or symbolic reading cannot account for these motion and placement verbs with a personal subject and a personal direct object.

The diabolos shows him all the kingdoms of the world, with G1166 attaching to the personal subject. Show-and-tell predicates require an agent who can intend a display, which is the grammar of a personal being.

Jesus dismisses the figure with a vocative, Hypage Satana, directly naming the same diabolos who has conducted the dialogue. A vocative of direct address presupposes a personal addressee, and it equates the Greek Satanas with the Hebrew adversary lexeme of Job and Zechariah.

Then the diabolos leaves him, aphiesin auton. The narrative records the agent departing, parallel to the satan going out in Job 1:12. The structural rhyme across Testaments, present, dialogue, depart, confirms a personal subject in both.

Satanas asks for the disciples to sift them like wheat, with G1809 the verb of formal request. To request is to intend, and to intend is to be a personal agent. The verb forecloses a non-personal reading.

The diabolos is called father, pater, and predicated as a murderer from the beginning, anthropoktonos ap arches, and a liar, pseustes. Personal-relational and moral nouns are predicated of him, and the temporal phrase from the beginning attributes a continuous history of acting, which only fits a personal being with a will.

Believers are to stand, G2476, against the methodeiai of the diabolos. Schemes are intended, not random, and are predicated of a personal possessor by the genitive tou diabolou. Methodeia is an agent noun for planned tactics.

The diabolos is your adversary, antidikos, prowling and seeking someone to devour. The legal-opponent noun antidikos plus verbs of prowling and seeking describe purposeful hostile activity, the opposer element of the proposition. The lion image is a comparison, hos leon, not an identity.

One referent is named four ways, the great dragon, the ancient serpent, ho kaloumenos Diabolos and ho Satanas, the one deceiving the whole world. The stacked appositional naming with the substantival participle ho planon unifies the Gen 3 serpent and the named adversary as a single acting being who is cast out, eblethe. Rev 20:2 repeats this fourfold identification.

The serpent, nachash, is the Subject of the speech verb amar and conducts a multi-turn dialogue with the woman. The serpent speaks, reasons, and contradicts a divine command, which is agent grammar. The text here does not lexically equate the serpent with the satan lexeme, so the identification with the named adversary is supplied later in the canon at Rev 12:9 and Rev 20:2.

complicating_texts.resolution: In Job and Zechariah the lexeme appears with the definite article, ha-satan, which reads as a title or office, the accuser or adversary, rather than as a personal proper name. This qualifies the name claim. It does not, however, complicate personhood, because the same articular form is the Subject of speech verbs, answers Yahweh, exercises a remit, and goes out, which are agent predicates. The article complicates onomastics, not ontology. By 1Chr.21.1 the form is anarthrous, and in the Greek New Testament the form Satanas is fully a proper name.

In Num.22.22 and Num.22.32 the noun satan is applied to the Angel of Yahweh as he stands in the way to oppose Balaam, and in 1Sam.29.4, 2Sam.19.22, and 1Kgs.11.14, 23, 25 it is applied to human opponents. This shows the lexeme has a common-noun sense, an adversary, that is not always the named figure. So the noun alone does not prove the named figure, but in Job 1 to 2, Zech 3, 1Chr 21, Ps 109, and the unified NT usage with G1228 and G4567, the same lexeme is attached by context, definite article, and stacked NT naming to one specific opposing personal agent.

The Gen 3 serpent is never lexically labeled satan or diabolos within the Hebrew text of the passage, so reading the serpent as the personal adversary is a cross-canonical inference rather than a direct lexical datum at Gen 3 itself. The link is supplied by Rev 12:9 and Rev 20:2, which name the ancient serpent, ho ophis ho archaios, as Diabolos and Satanas in the same noun phrase. Within Gen 3 itself only the personal-agent grammar of the speaking nachash is demonstrable.

The created element of the proposition, that this being is a creature with a beginning, is not carried by any anchor lemma in this bundle. The texts establish a personal opposing agent across both Testaments with dense recurring grammar, but they do not lexically assert his origin as created. Resolving the created clause would require traversal to creation-of-spirits, angelic-origin, and fall-of-angels texts that were not supplied here. It is therefore left unresolved on the lexical evidence at hand, flagged honestly, and does not subtract from the personal and opposing clauses.

variants.note: No variant units were supplied for the cited verses, and the bundle marks the question outside ECM scope. The four named figures in Rev 12:9 and Rev 20:2, the dialogue frames in Matt 4 and Luke 22:31, the predicates in John 8:44, and the council scene in Job 1 to 2 are textually stable in the supplied tradition. No plausible reading removes the personal agent.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Speech verbs, vocative address, multi-turn dialogue, possession, locomotion, scheming, and accusing are all predicated of the referent across both Testaments. The grammar required by these predicates is the grammar of a personal being who intends, speaks, and moves.

The articular Hebrew form ha-satan in Job 1 to 2 and Zech 3 supports reading satan as a function word, the accuser, in those passages, which qualifies the name claim. Personhood is left intact since the office is exercised by an acting subject who speaks and answers. The anarthrous 1Chr.21.1 and the Greek Satanas as a proper name show progressive movement from office to name across the canon.

A reader could ask whether the dialogue scenes in Job 1 to 2 and Matt 4 are dramatic personification of an impersonal evil principle, the way wisdom is personified in Prov 8. The lexical pattern resists this for three reasons named only from the words. First, the dialogues are multi-turn with two-way address and named vocatives, not monologues praising an attribute. Second, the same figure crosses Testaments under multiple lemmas, satan, diabolos, satanas, ophis, drakon, and these lemmas are stacked appositionally in Rev 12:9 and Rev 20:2 onto one referent. Third, the predicates include physical action verbs like G3880 take and G1166 show with personal direct objects, not the predicate types used for personified abstractions. The personification lens is therefore admissible as a question but is not sustainable as the dominant reading on this lexical pattern.

Outside the named-figure passages the noun satan is used of the Angel of Yahweh in Num 22 and of human opponents in 1 Sam, 2 Sam, and 1 Kgs, demonstrating a common-noun sense, an adversary. This is real polysemy. It does not undercut the personal-being clause for the named figure, because in Job 1 to 2, Zech 3, 1Chr 21:1, the NT use of G1228 and G4567, and the Rev 12:9 stack, context, articulation, and discourse role isolate the specific personal adversary.

hermeneutics.notes: The serpent of Gen 3 and the named adversary are joined by analogia scripturae through the appositional naming in Rev 12:9 and Rev 20:2. The move from articular ha-satan in the older texts to the anarthrous proper name Satanas in the Greek reflects progressive disclosure of the same figure rather than two different figures.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What does the canon say about the referent named by the lexemes satan and diabolos, regarding whether it acts as a personal agent, whether it opposes God and his people, and whether it is presented as a created spiritual being.
stem_audit.notes: The stem bundles three claims, personal, created, and opposing, and treats the created clause as settled. The lexical bundle strongly supports the personal and opposing clauses, with dense pan-canonical grammar, but does not directly witness the created clause, since no creation-of-spirits or angelic-origin lemma was supplied. The verdict is derived on the original stem, and the gap on the created clause is recorded honestly in complicating_texts and rationale rather than smuggled past.

lay_summary: The question asks whether Satan is a real, personal, created spiritual being who opposes God and his people. Looking only at the original-language words, the picture is consistent. The Hebrew word satan, H7854, the Greek words diabolos, G1228, and Satanas, G4567, attach to a figure who behaves like a person. In Job chapter 1 and 2 this figure comes into a gathering, is spoken to by Yahweh, and answers back across nine consecutive verses. The verbs of speaking and answering require someone who can be addressed and can reply. In Matthew chapter 4 the same figure approaches, speaks several times, takes Jesus to different places, shows him kingdoms, and finally departs, and Jesus turns and addresses him directly by name as Satan. Direct address by name only works toward a person, and physical-motion verbs like take and show point to an agent who intends an act. John chapter 8 calls him a father, a murderer from the beginning, and a liar, descriptions of a being with a will and a history. Luke chapter 22 has him asking to sift the disciples, which is a formal request that only a person can make. Ephesians chapter 6 has him owning schemes. First Peter chapter 5 names him an adversary who prowls and seeks someone to devour, and the roaring lion is a comparison there, not his nature. Revelation chapter 12 and chapter 20 gather four labels onto one figure, the dragon, the ancient serpent, the Devil, and Satan, the one who deceives the whole world, and this is what links the speaking serpent of Genesis chapter 3 to the named adversary. Two honest limits remain. In Job and Zechariah the word carries the article, the satan, which can read as a title, the accuser, though the same figure still speaks and acts as a person, and by First Chronicles 21 and in the New Testament the form is a proper name. And the word created is not proven by these particular texts, since none of the supplied words address his origin. So the words strongly support a real, personal, opposing being. The created part rests on wider teaching not contained in this set of texts and is flagged.
